```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Effect plots show how one smooth or parametric term contributes to the linear
predictor. To obtain the expected response in these examples, add the model
terms and intercept, then apply the inverse link. In the log-link model below,
that means exponentiating the sum to get mean carbon dioxide uptake. We use
the plant experiment from [Smooth trends and repeated measurements with
glmmTMB](glmmTMB-support.html) to plot curves for individual plants, then use
daily air quality measurements to plot interactions between continuous and
categorical predictors.

Load {gratia}, {mgcv} and {ggplot2} for the examples.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("ggplot2")
```

## Fit and plot plant-specific smooth curves

The carbon dioxide experiment measured uptake at seven concentrations on each
of twelve plants, with three plants per combination of origin and treatment.
The Gamma model with a log link keeps the fitted means positive and lets the
spread increase with the mean. In the model below, `s(log_conc)` allows the
shared uptake curve to level off as concentration increases. The `t2()` term
combines a spline for concentration with a plant random effect so that each
plant can have its own smooth departure from the shared curve.

```{r plant-flexible-fit}
plant <- as.data.frame(CO2)
plant$Plant <- factor(plant$Plant, ordered = FALSE)
plant$log_conc <- log(plant$conc) - mean(log(plant$conc))
plant_gam <- gam(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + s(log_conc, k = 5) +
    t2(log_conc, Plant, bs = c("cr", "re"), k = c(4, 12), full = TRUE),
  data = plant, family = Gamma(link = "log"), method = "REML")
overview(plant_gam)
```

The penalties pull plant-specific departures towards zero. With `full = TRUE`,
the model can penalise different parts of the tensor product separately. The
concentration basis is small because there are only seven observations per
plant. Use `re_levels` to plot the departures for three named plants from the
nonchilled Quebec group.

```{r plant-tensor-curves}
smooths(plant_gam)
draw(plant_gam, select = "t2(log_conc,Plant)",
  re_levels = list(Plant = c("Qn1", "Qn2", "Qn3")),
  xlab = "Centred log concentration", ylab = "Plant contribution to log uptake") &
  theme(legend.position = "right") & labs(colour = "Plant")
```

The concentration goes on the horizontal axis even if the plant factor comes
first in the tensor formula. `re_levels` selects which plants to display and
keeps their order from the fitted factor. To see the fitted mean for each
plant, plot the fitted values against the observations. These values combine
the shared curve, the plant's departure, the intercept and the terms for
origin and treatment before applying the inverse link. The concentration
units are microlitres per litre ($\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1}$), as reported
in Table 1 of the [original study](https://biology.mcgill.ca/faculty/potvin/articles/PotvinLech_90.pdf).

```{r plant-full-curves}
plant$mean_uptake <- fitted(plant_gam)
ggplot(plant, aes(conc, uptake, group = Plant, colour = Treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean_uptake)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Type) +
  labs(x = expression(CO[2] ~ concentration ~ (mu * L ~ L^{-1})),
    y = expression(CO[2] ~ uptake ~ (mu * mol ~ m^{-2} ~ s^{-1})))
```

The fitted curves rise rapidly and then flatten for these plants. They include
each plant's estimated departure. At the group level, the model assumes the
same concentration response shape for all combinations of origin and
treatment, with group differences entering as multipliers of mean uptake.
Use `variance_comp()` to extract the variance components for the penalties
on the shared smooth and the plant-specific departures.

```{r plant-variance-components}
variance_comp(plant_gam)
```

The spline rows describe how strongly the model penalises different parts of
the fitted curves. The `scale` row estimates the Gamma dispersion. Multiplying
it by the squared fitted mean gives the estimated variance of uptake around
that mean.

## Fit temperature, wind and month interactions

The `airquality` data contain daily New York measurements from May to September
1973. Ozone is in parts per billion, temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, wind
speed in miles per hour, and solar radiation in Langleys; see
`?datasets::airquality` for the sources. We retain complete cases, so our
analysis uses the days with all needed measurements.

The question is whether ozone's association with temperature depends on wind,
and whether that relationship is stable across summer months. We model log
ozone with a Gaussian distribution, allow a smooth association with solar
radiation, and use a temperature-by-wind-by-month interaction.

```{r ozone-fit}
ozone <- na.omit(airquality[c("Ozone", "Solar.R", "Wind", "Temp", "Month")])
ozone$month <- factor(ozone$Month, labels = month.abb[5:9])
contrasts(ozone$month) <- contr.treatment(levels(ozone$month))
ozone_gam <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R, k = 6) + Temp * Wind * month,
  data = ozone, method = "REML")
table(ozone$month)
overview(ozone_gam)
```

A three-way interaction gives each month its own temperature-by-wind surface.
Estimates can be imprecise where a month has few observations at similar
temperatures and wind speeds. Plot those observations before interpreting
the fitted surfaces.

```{r ozone-support}
ggplot(ozone, aes(Temp, Wind, colour = Ozone)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)",
    colour = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

## Plot the separate interaction contributions

Start with the temperature-by-wind interaction for May, the reference month.
`parametric_terms()` lists the available terms; `parametric_effects()` evaluates
the chosen contribution on a grid for plotting.

```{r ozone-numeric-interaction}
parametric_terms(ozone_gam)
weather_effect <- parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:Wind", n_2d = 30)
draw(weather_effect, surface = "tile") &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")
```

Each point on the surface shows the fitted coefficient for `Temp:Wind`
multiplied by the temperature and wind speed. The colours show how much this
term adds to or subtracts from fitted **log** ozone. This is the interaction
for May and the starting point for the other months' interactions.

`surface = "tile"` uses vector rectangles, which can be useful in a vector
figure. The default `"raster"` keeps large plots compact. `n_2d = 30` evaluates
30 points along each surface axis. Increase `n_2d` for a finer display of the
same fitted surface. Next plot how each month's temperature-by-wind
interaction differs from May's.

```{r ozone-month-interactions, fig.height = 7}
draw(parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:Wind:month", n_2d = 25),
  surface = "tile") &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")
```

The model uses treatment contrasts with May as the reference month, so the
adjustment is zero in May. The panels share a colour scale centred at zero.
`dist` controls how far a grid point can be from the observations before it
is hidden, after scaling the two axes to range from zero to one. This uses
observations from all months. Use the monthly scatterplots above to see which
parts of each surface are supported by observations from that month.

Plot the temperature-by-month interaction to see how it adjusts the main
temperature slope. Each month has its own straight line because the term is
linear in temperature.

```{r ozone-numeric-factor}
draw(parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:month")) &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Additional contribution to log ozone")
```

These slopes must be combined with the reference temperature slope and the
wind interactions to describe the model's temperature association. The
[conditional comparisons article](prediction-comparisons.html) shows how to
compare complete fitted values without isolating contrast-coded terms.

For a direct view of the complete model, predict at observed weather conditions:

```{r ozone-full-predictions}
ozone$fitted_log <- fitted(ozone_gam)
ggplot(ozone, aes(log(Ozone), fitted_log, colour = month)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Observed log ozone", y = "Fitted log ozone", colour = "Month")
```

The plot shows how closely the fitted mean **log** ozone follows the observed
log concentrations. Under this model, exponentiating the fitted values gives
the conditional median ozone concentration. To calculate the conditional
arithmetic mean on the original scale, also account for the residual variance
on the log scale. Similar residuals on nearby days could affect the uncertainty
in monthly comparisons, so check residuals against the observation dates.

## Show an interaction surface in three dimensions

The optional {ggcube} package can show the same numerical surface in three
dimensions:

```{r ozone-3d}
if (requireNamespace("ggcube", quietly = TRUE)) {
  draw(weather_effect, surface = "3d",
    surface_3d = list(yaw = 35, persp = FALSE)) &
    labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")
}
```

Height and fill both represent the same partial contribution. Use the flat
plots with their common colour scale to compare surfaces across months.

Parametric effect plots use the model's covariate scale by default.
For example, a term involving `log(x)` uses `log(x)` on the horizontal axis.
`back_transform = TRUE` displays original covariate coordinates without
changing effect values or intervals. With saved smooth estimates, prepare
them using `smooth_estimates(model, back_transform = TRUE)` before asking
`draw()` to use that scale. See the
[article on transformed covariates](transformed-covariates.html) for worked
examples, including transformations without an analytic inverse.

By default, the intervals include uncertainty in the intercept and its
covariance with the plotted term. Set `overall_uncertainty = FALSE` for
intervals that reflect uncertainty in the term alone. An interval for the
difference between two predictions needs to account for their covariance.
